hero.role: Digital Business & AI · Data analysis · Bern
hero.intro: I enjoy working with data, mathematics and tricky questions. Here I show projects I have worked on: what they do, how they work and what I found out along the way.
about.title: About me
about.lead: I love data, mathematics and complex problems, especially when the solution does something good for people and nature.
about.path1: It all started with an online game. When I was about ten or twelve, I traded there: watching prices, doing the maths and trying to make the best possible deals. I had little money and little time, so I had to think carefully about when something was worth it. Somehow that fascinated me more than the game itself.
about.path2: Because I enjoyed calculating and working with numbers, I later chose a commercial apprenticeship at a bank. There I realised that everyday work was shaped far more by advising customers than I had expected. So I completed the Passerelle, a university entrance programme, and started studying physics. I liked the mathematics, but I missed the practical application.
about.path3: Today I study Digital Business & AI at Bern University of Applied Sciences (BFH), focusing on data analysis. Here I can combine what already interested me back then: working with numbers, recognising patterns and turning them into something that is useful beyond the screen.
about.p3: I find balance in endurance sports: I train for triathlon up to the Ironman distance, preferably outdoors in nature.
projects.title: Projects
bors.alt: BORS web app: map of Bern with streets coloured green, yellow or red depending on passability
bors.text: Routing for emergency vehicles: which street is physically passable for which vehicle? For an emergency doctor's car, an ambulance and two fire engines, BORS checks whether width, height and weight are sufficient and calculates the route on that basis, in Bern and ten neighbouring municipalities.
bors.role: My part: the entire technical implementation, from data preparation and width measurement to the router and the web app.
bors.routeAlt: Example route to the Felsenau bridge: the large fire engine takes a 6.8 km detour
bors.routeCap: Example Felsenau bridge: the emergency doctor and the ambulance drive directly, the large fire engine needs a 6.8 km detour.
bors.netAlt: Entire BORS street network, coloured by status for the large fire engine
bors.netCap: The whole network for the large fire engine: green validated, yellow unvalidated, red blocked.
bors.s1p: A normal navigation app calculates for cars, not for a three-metre-wide fire engine. So which streets work for which vehicle?
bors.s2p: The usable width of a street is not directly available in any data source. Parking spaces, walls and pillars narrow it, and every measurement has a tolerance. Height and weight limits from OpenStreetMap are not confirmed on site.
bors.s3p: I measure the width from the official cadastral survey using cross-sections and subtract a measurement tolerance for each street edge. Each street gets one of three states per vehicle: validated, unvalidated or blocked. Routing first uses only validated streets.
bors.s3p2: One decision along the way: rather mark a street as “unvalidated” than promise false certainty. If there is no validated path, BORS shows an alternative route, marks it and counts uncertain sections with double the time.
bors.s4h: What has been checked and what has not
bors.s4p: Checked: the web app calculates exactly like the router in QGIS; 325 out of 325 test routes are identical.
bors.s4p2: Not checked: BORS has not been tested in real operations or systematically on site. It is a prototype that is not approved for operational use.
bors.s5p: BORS can make bottlenecks for large vehicles visible in advance. Whether it saves time in real operations is still open. The next step would be to check critical spots on site.
sm.alt: SplitMate debt overview: total 20 CHF, two people each pay 10 CHF to a third
sm.text: A web app that lets a shared flat split its costs fairly: create a group, record expenses, and the app shows who owes whom how much.
sm.role: My part: debt calculation in the backend and frontend setup.
sm.startAlt: SplitMate start page with forms to create or join a group
sm.startCap: Start page: create a group or join with a code.
sm.arch1: Frontend: Vue 3 with Vue Router, built with Vite.
sm.arch2: Backend: Strapi 5 as a REST API, data in SQLite.
sm.arch3: Communication: the frontend calls the API with fetch(). On login, Strapi returns a JWT token.
sm.arch4: Custom endpoint: GET /api/expenses/schulden calculates the debts on the server and returns a list of payments.
sm.calc1: Add up what each person has paid.
sm.calc2: Split the total evenly: balance = paid − share.
sm.calc3: Settle debtors and creditors one after the other until all balances are zero. This needs at most one payment fewer than there are people.
sm.limits: Today the calculation splits all expenses evenly among the people who paid something themselves, and not yet per group. As a next step it would have to calculate per group and take into account who an expense was for.
r.alt: Scatter plot: life expectancy falls as the share of smokers rises, more steeply in high-income regions
r.meta: Group project · Data Management & Data Analysis
r.title: Data analysis: life expectancy (R)
r.text: Regression models on the relationship between life expectancy, share of smokers and income in 100 US regions.
r.result: Smoking lowers life expectancy, and in higher-income regions this effect is stronger (interaction share of smokers × income). I checked the models with residual diagnostics.
